# Narrative Structure

## Purpose

Hold the shape of the story at three scales: the whole series, each issue,
and each page. Acts and turning points decide what an issue has to contain.
Page budgets decide how much room each beat gets. Page turns decide where a
reveal lands, because a reader sees two facing pages at once and only the
turn hides anything.

## Use When

- Compiling or updating the story bible after source analysis.
- Dividing the story into issues for the series plan.
- Breaking one issue into scenes and beats with a page budget per beat.
- A rewrite moves a turning point and the pages after it need rechecking.

## Inputs

- `production/story/story-bible.yaml`: `facts`, `timeline`, `characters`.
- `production/project.yaml`: `comic_format`, `publication`,
  `reading_direction`.
- `production/story/series-plan.yaml` and `issues/<ISS_ID>/issue.yaml` when
  they exist.
- Scene files under `issues/<ISS_ID>/scenes/` when updating a breakdown.

## Process

1. State the spine: the protagonist, what they want, what stands in the way,
   and the question the ending answers. Write it into `premise` and into
   each character's `arc`.
2. Mark the turning points against `timeline` order numbers. A turning point
   is an event that exists in the registry, never a page-count guess.
3. Divide the story into issues. Each issue ends on a turn: a decision, a
   reversal, or a sharper question. Fill `series-plan.yaml` per issue with
   `id`, `number`, `title`, `source_span`, `summary`, `page_budget`, and
   `status`.
4. Set page budgets from the publication type. A strip is one page. A
   one-shot usually runs 8 to 24 pages and a periodical issue 20 to 24. A
   webtoon episode is counted in scroll segments. Then budget inside the
   issue: turning-point beats get the most pages, transit gets the fewest.
5. Break the issue into scenes (one location, one stretch of time) and beats.
   Each beat in the scene file gets a `summary` and the `pages` it occupies.
   Give every beat one function: setup, escalation, reversal, revelation, or
   release. A beat with no function is flagged for cutting.
6. Build the setup and payoff table. For every planted object, line, image,
   or injury, record the page where it is drawn and the page where it pays
   off. The setup has to be visible in a panel on an earlier page; a flare
   gun fired on page 9 is seen in the wheelhouse on page 1. Keep the table
   in the story bible's `notes` and name the function in each page's
   `purpose`.
7. Place the page turns (paged format). In a left-to-right book, odd pages
   sit on the right and the turn comes after them. Put the question in the
   last panel of the right-hand page (`page_turn: cliffhanger` or `reveal`)
   and the answer in the first panel of the next left-hand page. Mirror this
   for `reading_direction: rtl`. A spread (`spread_with`) starts on a
   left-hand page. A webtoon has no turns: distance of scroll does the
   hiding (`rules/webtoon/scroll-grammar.md`).
8. Check the pacing. Rate tension per beat from 1 to 5 and look for runs of
   more than three pages at one level. Check panel density too: many small
   panels slow a moment down, one large panel stops the reader on it, and
   the same grid on every page flattens both effects.
9. Check the last page of each issue. It closes on an image, and that image
   answers the issue's question or sharpens it for the next one.
10. Confirm the arithmetic: the beats' page lists add up to `page_count` in
    `issue.yaml`, which matches `page_budget` in the series plan.

## Outputs

- `production/story/story-bible.yaml`: `premise`, `characters[].arc`,
  `timeline[].issue`, and the setup and payoff table in `notes`.
- `production/story/series-plan.yaml` (`series-plan` schema).
- Beat functions and page budgets in `issues/<ISS_ID>/scenes/<SC_ID>.yaml`,
  and `page_turn` guidance that `/page-plan` writes into each `page.yaml`.

## Quality Bar

- Beat page lists add up to the issue's `page_count`, and that equals the
  series plan's `page_budget` or the difference is explained.
- Every beat has exactly one function.
- Every setup has a payoff page or an explicit `unresolved` note, and the
  setup page comes first.
- Every `reveal` or `cliffhanger` sits on a page the reader turns: a
  right-hand page in a left-to-right paged comic.
- Turning points cite timeline order numbers and beat IDs that exist.

## Common Failure Modes

- Forcing three acts onto material with a different shape. A four-page
  short has a setup, a turn, and an ending, and that is enough.
- Budgeting pages evenly, so the climax gets the same room as a walk along
  the deck.
- A reveal on a right-hand page, visible from the facing page before the
  reader gets there.
- A payoff whose setup exists only in a caption and was never drawn.
- An issue that ends where the page count ran out.
- A spread planned across a turn, right-hand page then left-hand page, so
  the two halves are never seen together.
- Rewriting story facts while annotating them. Structure works on the
  registry as it stands; changes go through `adaptation`.

## Notes

Very short forms have their own shapes. A strip is a setup, a turn, and a
last panel that lands, in three or four panels. A one-page story spends its
top tier on the situation and its bottom-right panel on the ending, since
that is where the eye finishes.

Page-level craft that both formats share lives in `rules/layout/pacing.md`.
The turn itself is covered by `rules/paged/page-turn-grammar.md`.
